meaning: How many audio measurements (samples) are taken per second. Speech models use 16,000 Hz; codecs often 24,000 Hz. The highest frequency you can capture is half the sample rate (the Nyquist limit).
A frequency above half the sample rate doesn't disappear: it folds back and shows up as a fake lower pitch. Recorders and resamplers low-pass filter first to prevent it.
Cut audio into short overlapping windows (e.g. 25 ms every 10 ms), taper each with a Hann window and take its FFT. The magnitudes, stacked over time, form a spectrogram.
A picture of sound: time on the x-axis, frequency on the y-axis, loudness as brightness. Lets CNNs and transformers treat audio like an image.

A pitch scale matched to human hearing (roughly linear below 1 kHz, logarithmic above). A mel filterbank of overlapping triangles turns FFT bins into 80 or 128 mel rows, with more detail at low frequencies.
A mel spectrogram on a logarithmic (decibel-like) scale, so quiet sounds are visible and volume changes become shifts. The standard input to speech recognition (Whisper: 80 × 3,000 per 30 s).
Mel-frequency cepstral coefficients: a cosine transform of each log-mel column, keeping about a dozen numbers that describe the spectrum's shape. The classic pre-deep-learning speech feature.
Data augmentation for speech: warp the log-mel picture in time and blank out random frequency bands and time slices during training, so the model learns redundant cues.

A loss for sequence labelling without frame-level labels: the network outputs a symbol (or blank) per frame, and the loss sums the probability of every frame string that collapses to the transcript, using dynamic programming.
CTC's extra “nothing new here” symbol. Decoding merges repeated symbols and then drops blanks; a blank between two identical letters is what keeps doubles like the “ll” in hello.
Take the most likely symbol at each frame, then collapse (merge repeats, drop blanks). Fast enough for streaming; beam search with a language model is the more accurate alternative.

Self-supervised speech pretraining (Meta, 2020): a CNN encodes raw audio, spans are masked, and a transformer must identify the true quantized latent among distractors. Fine-tuned with CTC, 10 minutes of labels reached 4.8% / 8.2% WER on LibriSpeech.
A streaming ASR model that, unlike CTC, also conditions each output on the previous outputs through a prediction network. TDT variants also predict how many frames to skip.
A speech encoder block that combines self-attention (global context) with a convolution module (local patterns). Common encoder for CTC, transducer and encoder–decoder ASR.

OpenAI's encoder–decoder transformer ASR trained on 680,000 hours of weakly labelled web audio. Special tokens choose language, transcribe vs translate, and timestamps; it works on 30-second log-mel windows and can hallucinate during silence.
(substitutions + deletions + insertions) ÷ words in the reference, after aligning with minimum edits and normalizing text. Lower is better; insertions can push it above 100%.
Phonemes are the sound units of a language (HH AH L OW). A grapheme-to-phoneme (G2P) model converts spelling to phonemes before text-to-speech.

In non-autoregressive TTS (FastSpeech), a small network predicts how many frames each phoneme lasts; the length regulator repeats each phoneme's vector that many times so all frames can be generated in parallel. Scaling durations changes speaking speed.
The model that turns a mel spectrogram (no phase) back into a waveform. WaveNet did it one sample at a time; HiFi-GAN does it in parallel, much faster than real time.

Generation (or transcription) time divided by audio length; below 1 is faster than real time. Leaderboards often report the inverse, RTFx. Driven mostly by the number of sequential steps per second of audio.

An autoencoder for sound (SoundStream, EnCodec, Mimi): a strided-conv encoder, a quantizer that turns each frame into a few integers, and a decoder, trained with GAN losses. Its integers are audio tokens.
Quantize a vector in stages: each codebook quantizes what the previous stages missed. Bits add up while codebook sizes stay small, and dropping later stages lowers the bitrate.

Semantic tokens (from a self-supervised speech model) capture what is said; acoustic codec tokens capture how it sounds. AudioLM generates semantic tokens first for coherence, then acoustic ones for quality.
A transformer that generates audio as codec tokens, like an LLM generates text. VALL-E used one for zero-shot TTS from a 3-second voice prompt.
A model that listens and speaks at the same time by modelling the user's and its own audio streams in parallel (Moshi: 12.5 Hz, 160 ms theoretical latency), so interruptions need no turn logic.
An image encoder (CLIP or SigLIP ViT) plus a connector plus an LLM, so the LLM can read image tokens next to text tokens.
A linear layer or small MLP that maps image-encoder vectors into the LLM's embedding space (LLaVA). Trained first on image–caption pairs with both big models frozen.
BLIP-2's small transformer with 32 learned queries that cross-attend to frozen image features and hand a fixed 32 vectors to a frozen LLM, whatever the image size.

Ways to read big images: cut them into encoder-sized tiles plus a thumbnail (LLaVA-NeXT, InternVL) or let the ViT take any size and merge 2×2 patches into one token (Qwen2-VL). Token cost grows with pixels, so cap it.

Training one model on mixed text and image tokens from the start (Chameleon: 1,024 discrete tokens per 512² image) instead of bolting a vision encoder onto a pretrained LLM. Can read and generate images.
A VLM describing objects that aren't in the image, usually because the language prior wins. POPE measures it with yes/no questions about present and absent objects (random, popular, adversarial).
